title: All Paths From Source to Target
statement:
A directed graph with `n` nodes, numbered `0` to `n - 1`, is described by `graph`: for every node `i`, `graph[i]` lists the nodes that have an edge coming from `i` (an edge `i -> graph[i][j]`). The graph has no cycles.

Return every distinct path that starts at node `0` and ends at node `n - 1`, each written as the list of nodes it visits in order. The paths may be returned in any order. If node `n - 1` cannot be reached from node `0`, return an empty list.
constraints: graph[i][j] != i (no edge from a node to itself)
The values in each graph[i] are distinct
The graph is a directed acyclic graph (DAG)
notes:
## Intuition

Because the graph has no cycles, a walk that follows edges can never come back to a node it already used, so no "visited" set is needed: every route that leaves `0` and reaches `n - 1` is automatically a valid, simple path. The task is just to list all such routes, which is exactly what a depth-first search with backtracking does. A slower but equally correct idea is to grow every partial path one edge at a time, layer by layer, keeping the ones that hit `n - 1`.

## Approach

1. Let `target` be `n - 1`. Keep `path`, the nodes on the current route (starting as `[0]`), and `paths`, the finished routes.
2. `explore(node)` is called with `node` already at the end of `path`.
3. If `node` is `target`, save a copy of `path` and return.
4. Otherwise, for each `next` in `graph[node]`: push it, call `explore(next)`, then pop it so the next neighbour can take its place.
5. Call `explore(0)` and return `paths`.

## Example 1, step by step

`graph = [[1,2],[3],[3],[]]`, so `target = 3`.

- From 0 go to 1 (`path = [0,1]`), then to 3 (`[0,1,3]`): the target, so it is saved. Pop back to `[0]`.
- From 0 go to 2 (`[0,2]`), then to 3 (`[0,2,3]`): saved again.

Result: `[[0,1,3],[0,2,3]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(2^n · n): a DAG on `n` nodes can hold up to 2^(n-2) source-to-target paths, and each saved path costs up to `n` to copy.
- Space: O(n) for `path` and the recursion depth, plus the output itself.

## Pitfalls

- Push a **copy** of `path`; the array keeps changing as the search continues.
- Forgetting `path.pop()` leaves old nodes on the route and corrupts every later path.
- Do not stop at the first time a node is reached: the same node may lie on many different paths, so no visited marking is used.
- Node `n - 1` may be unreachable; the answer is then an empty list.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `target` | the destination node `n - 1` |
| `paths` | every complete path found |
| `path` | the nodes on the current route, starting with 0 |
| `node` | the node the search is standing on |
| `next` | a neighbour of `node` being tried |

narration.2: The destination is the last node, n - 1.
narration.3: paths collects every complete route from 0 to the destination.
narration.4: path holds the current route; every route begins at node 0.
narration.6: explore continues the route from node, which is already the last entry of path.
narration.7: Reaching the destination means path is a complete answer.
narration.8: Save a copy, because path will keep changing.
narration.9: No need to go further: the route ends here.
narration.11: Try every edge leaving the current node.
narration.12: Extend the route with this neighbour.
narration.13: Search onward from the neighbour; the graph has no cycles, so this always terminates.
narration.14: Undo the step so the next neighbour can be tried instead.
narration.19: Every route to the destination has been collected.
